newsitem.title: USA: Key senator concerned about balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Key senator concerned about balanced budget.

text.p: A pivotal Democratic senator Monday expressed her concerns about voting for a Republican-authored balanced budget amendment, raising doubts that it would pass the Senate.

Louisiana's Mary Landrieu told reporters she would announce her decision shortly, possibly Tuesday. Democrats need only one more vote to deprive Republicans of victory for their constitutional amendment. Both sides have been anxiously awaiting decisions by Landrieu and freshman Democrat Robert Torricelli of New Jersey, both publicly undecided.
"I have reservations because it does not provide for a capital budget. I have reservations because Social Security was established as a trust fund and it is not operating as one," she told reporters.

Landrieu said she felt two Democratic alternatives to come before the Senate would address these problems -- establishment of a capital budget to pay for long-term government investments and the exclusion of the retirement funds from the annual budget calculation.

But only the Republican version is thought to have a chance of winning the 67 votes required to pass. Constitutional amendments must have a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate and must be ratified by 38 of 50 states.
She said that she did not expect Louisiana voters to consider that she broke a campaign promise if her decision is to oppose the Republican amendment.

"I committed to vote for an amendment, not for a particular version. I think voters want me to vote for the best amendment I can vote for," Landrieu said. She spoke to a small group of reporters off the Senate floor.

Meanwhile, as the lengthy Senate debate rolled on, Republicans accused Democrats of using the popular Social Security system as political cover for votes against the balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

Republicans have made the balanced budget amendment their No. 1 political goal this year and thought chances of passage were excellent after November's election produced a larger Republican majority and more Democrat supporters.

Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch, Republican of Utah, called a news conference to counter Democratic charges that Social Security's retirement benefits would be jeopardized if his party succeeded in passing the balanced budget amendment.

"Talk about a gimmick," Hatch said. "This is a phony issue. It has been exploited for the last ten years," he said, adding that opponents were raising fears about solvency of the retirement fund as a way to kill the amendment. The Senate is to vote either this week or next.

Hatch remained optimistic that it would pass, although Democratic leaders put its chances at 50-50 and House leaders postponed their vote indefinitely due to fears the Republican version could not pass.
Republicans said the Social Security system, which will begin to run deficits around 2019, will be better off if the budget is balanced and the economy improves than if deficits continue to grow.

"There is no argument against this, except that you want to spend more, you want to tax more," Hatch said later on the Senate floor. "Only in Washington, D.C., only in this god-forsaken town ... do people believe a $107 billion deficit for a fiscal year is wonderful," he said.
Sen. Harry Reid, a Nevada Democrat, charged Republicans aimed to use the balanced budget amendment as a wedge to start cutting Social Security benefits in the next century.

The Senate will vote Tuesday on Reid's amendment to exempt Social Security from the deficit calculation. Several other amendments to permit exceptions during economic downturns or for other reasons will be considered later in the week.

The balanced budget amendment requires the government balance its budget annually starting in 2002 or when it is ratified by 38 of 50 states. It must pass the House and Senate by two-thirds majority vote. It would not bar red ink but would make it more difficult for Congress to approve deficit spending, higher taxes and borrowing.
